transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Well… what finally made me come in is that my concentration has gotten, I guess, unreliable. That’s the best word I can think of. I’m a dentist, and I’ll be at the clinic reviewing a chart—something I’ve done thousands of times—and then I realize I’ve read the same line two or three times and I still haven’t taken it in, because my mind has wandered off to everything that could go wrong.

And it’s not just at work. I paint watercolors, and I’ll be laying out a wash, trying to focus on the color and the timing, and then suddenly I’m not really there with it. I’m off in my head running through worries, possibilities, little disasters that haven’t happened. It’s frustrating, because I’ve always thought of myself as fairly careful and attentive, and now I don’t feel like I can count on that in the same way.
Do you find yourself worrying excessively about many different things?

Yes… yes, I do. It’s not just one thing, which is part of what bothers me. If it were just, say, money, I could at least point to it and say, “All right, that’s the problem.” But my mind keeps circling around all sorts of things.

I worry about whether my old patients are being looked after properly, even when I don’t really have a reason to think they aren’t. I worry about the handoff of the practice—whether it was financially sound, whether I missed something, whether I made a mistake that won’t show up until later. And then it jumps to bigger, more personal things, like whether I’m going to become sort of useless once I’m fully retired, like I won’t know what to do with myself or have any value if I’m not working the way I always have.

And the thing is, even to me it feels out of proportion. I can hear myself sometimes and think, “This is too much, you don’t need to be going over this again,” but it doesn’t really stop just because I’ve noticed that.
Did these worries begin after you retired or started handing off your practice?

Yes, it really started around then—when I began the formal process of retiring and handing off the practice. That was about a year and three months ago now, maybe a little over, depending on where I count it from. Before that I could worry, of course, but it didn’t have this same constant quality. Once the retirement became real and not just something “down the road,” my mind seemed to latch onto it and then branch out from there.
When the worries start, do you find it hard to stop or control them?

Yes, very much so. That’s probably one of the things that bothers me most about it, actually. I can usually tell myself, logically, “All right, you’ve thought this through. There’s nothing else to do right now.” I try to talk to myself almost the way I’d talk to a nervous patient in the chair—calmly, step by step, reassuring them that we’ve checked what needs to be checked.

But it doesn’t seem to hold. One concern sort of opens the door to the next one. I’ll think, “Did I answer that email clearly enough?” and then I’m checking my inbox. Then I’ll remember some note or record and feel like I should review it. Or I’ll ask the same question again, even though I know I’ve already asked and gotten an answer. It’s like I’m looking for certainty, but the certainty doesn’t stick for very long.

So yes, I do try to stop it. It’s not that I just give myself over to it willingly. I try to reason it away, but it keeps moving to the next thing, and before I know it I’m still in it instead of letting it go.
For the past 6 months, have you been worrying like this on most days?

Yes, definitely. For the past six months, it’s been most days—really, it goes back further than that. It started when I began the formal retirement process and handing things over, which was about a year and three months ago.

At first I think I told myself it was just the normal stress of a big life transition, but it didn’t really settle. It became this ongoing pattern, day after day, where the worrying was just sort of there in the background or would flare up over some detail. So yes, six months is absolutely true, but it’s been more like fifteen months altogether.
Do you often feel physically tense or keyed up?

I’m not completely sure how to answer that, actually. I mean, I wouldn’t say I walk around feeling physically tense all the time in a dramatic way, like shaking or anything obvious. But if you mean more like feeling wound up, or like my body doesn’t quite settle when my mind is going, then… yes, maybe at times.

I notice it more when I stop and pay attention. My shoulders might be up, or my jaw feels a little tight, and I have to remind myself to relax. But I’m not always sure whether that’s from the worrying itself or just years of being used to holding myself a certain way, you know, working in close quarters and concentrating. So I don’t want to overstate it.

“Keyed up” is probably a fair word sometimes, though. Not panicky, exactly. More like I’m braced for something, even when there isn’t anything immediate happening.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

Yes, I have. That’s been one of the more frustrating parts, because I’ll feel tired by the time I get into bed—properly tired, like I should just be able to close my eyes and be done for the day. But then as soon as the house is quiet and there’s nothing else to distract me, my mind seems to start up again.

I’ll lie there replaying things about patient transfers—whether I explained something clearly enough, whether the handoff was complete, whether someone might run into a problem because I missed some detail. And then it can shift into money things, retirement details, accounts, whether I’ve planned properly. It’s not necessarily one big thought; it’s more like a whole chain of them.

And even when I do fall asleep, it doesn’t always feel like restful sleep. I’m often awake around four or five in the morning, and then that same mental list is right there waiting for me. I’ll feel as if I never really settled, like I was only half-asleep or still working on problems in the background. So yes, sleep has definitely been affected.
Have you been feeling down or depressed?

I’m not sure I’d call it depressed, exactly. I mean, I do get discouraged, and there are days where I feel worn down by it all, like I’m not quite myself. But “down or depressed” feels like a strong word, and I don’t know that it fits in the way you might mean clinically.

It’s more that I feel preoccupied and tired of my own thoughts, if that makes sense. Sometimes I’m less enthusiastic about things than I used to be, but I can’t tell if that’s sadness or just being mentally drained. I haven’t really thought of myself as depressed. Maybe frustrated, unsettled, a bit heavy at times—but I’m not sure I’d say depressed.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy, like painting?

I’m not sure I’d say I’ve lost pleasure in it, no. Painting is a bit tricky for me to answer about, because it’s always been something I do in fits and starts anyway. It’s not like I had a strict schedule where every Saturday afternoon I painted and now I suddenly don’t.

I still like the idea of it, and when I actually get myself set up, I can enjoy parts of it—the colors, the focus of it, the way time can pass differently. But I suppose I don’t reach for it as readily as I used to. Whether that’s loss of interest or just being distracted and not making the space for it, I honestly don’t know.

So… I wouldn’t say painting feels pointless or that I get no enjoyment from it. It’s more that I’m not always in the frame of mind to start.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot about things unrelated to retirement or the practice handoff?

Yes… yes, I do. It isn’t only the retirement paperwork or the handoff, although those are the easiest examples because they’re right in front of me. My mind tends to circle outward from there.

I’ll start with something concrete, like whether my old patients are being looked after properly, whether the records are clear enough, whether someone will need context that only I would have remembered. Then it becomes the financial side of the practice handoff—whether it was structured sensibly, whether I missed something, whether it’ll hold up the way I thought it would.

But then it drifts into larger, less solvable things. I’ll worry about what I’m going to be once I’m fully retired, whether I’ll become sort of… irrelevant, I suppose. Useless is the word that comes to mind, though I don’t like saying it. And I can recognize, at least part of the time, that the amount of worrying I’m doing is probably out of proportion. It’s not as if there’s always a new emergency. It’s more that my mind keeps treating everything like it might become one.
In the past two weeks, have you felt sad or low most of the day nearly every day?

I don’t think so—not most of the day, nearly every day. I mean, I’ve had low moments, certainly. There are times when I feel sort of flat or discouraged, and I can sit with a heavy feeling for a while, especially if I’m thinking too much about things. But if you’re asking whether I’ve been sad in that sustained, all-day way, day after day, I don’t think that’s quite right.

It’s more intermittent, I suppose. It comes and goes. Some mornings I feel a bit burdened, or I notice I’m not as light as I’d like to be, but then I can get pulled into something and not feel exactly sad. So… no, I wouldn’t say sad or low most of the day nearly every day.
If retirement and handing off your practice had not been happening, do you think this level of worrying would still be there?

I think… yes, unfortunately, some version of it would still be there. The retirement and the handoff have definitely given my mind something very obvious to latch onto, so I don’t want to pretend they’re irrelevant. They’re real concerns, and there are practical details involved.

But the level of worrying feels bigger than just those things. My mind keeps circling around all sorts of things—whether my old patients are being looked after properly, whether the practice handoff is financially sound, whether I’ve missed something important, and then it shifts into this larger fear of what I’ll be once I’m fully retired. Whether I’ll become useless, I suppose.

And even as I’m saying it, part of me can hear that it’s out of proportion. Not completely irrational, maybe, but more intense and persistent than the situation really calls for. So yes, I think if retirement weren’t happening, my mind would probably find something else to chew on. That’s what worries me, actually—the way it seems to keep looking for the next thing.
Do you feel these worries are mainly a reaction to your retirement and handing off the practice?

Not mainly, no. I mean, they’re certainly part of it, and I don’t want to minimize that. Retirement and handing off the practice are big changes, and they’ve given my mind plenty of material to work with.

But the worrying doesn’t feel confined to that. It spreads. I’ll start with whether my old patients are being cared for properly, then whether the handoff was financially sound, whether I missed some detail I should have caught, and then before I know it I’m thinking about what I’ll be once I’m fully retired—whether I’ll become useless, basically.

And even to me, it feels out of proportion. That’s the uncomfortable part. I can see that some concern is reasonable, but the way my mind keeps circling around it again and again feels like more than just a normal reaction to retirement.

doctor.question: If retirement and handing off your practice had not been happening, do you think this level of worrying would still be there?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: My mind keeps circling around all sorts of things—whether my old patients are being looked after properly, whether the practice handoff is financially sound, whether I’ll become useless once I’m fully retired—and the worry feels out of proportion even to me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the worrying is limited to retirement/practice handoff or would persist more broadly, which directly assesses excessive anxiety and worry across events or activities.

patient.answer:
I think… yes, unfortunately, some version of it would still be there. The retirement and the handoff have definitely given my mind something very obvious to latch onto, so I don’t want to pretend they’re irrelevant. They’re real concerns, and there are practical details involved.

But the level of worrying feels bigger than just those things. My mind keeps circling around all sorts of things—whether my old patients are being looked after properly, whether the practice handoff is financially sound, whether I’ve missed something important, and then it shifts into this larger fear of what I’ll be once I’m fully retired. Whether I’ll become useless, I suppose.

And even as I’m saying it, part of me can hear that it’s out of proportion. Not completely irrational, maybe, but more intense and persistent than the situation really calls for. So yes, I think if retirement weren’t happening, my mind would probably find something else to chew on. That’s what worries me, actually—the way it seems to keep looking for the next thing.

inference.note: Ruled down F32.9: patient denies depressed mood most of the day nearly every day and does not endorse clear anhedonia; symptoms are dominated by excessive, hard-to-control worry across multiple domains for >6 months, making F41.1 most likely. F43.2 remains possible given onset around retirement transition, though persistence, generalization beyond the stressor, and probable continuation without it argue against it as primary.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the anxiety is primarily an excessive response to an identifiable stressor, which would support adjustment disorder over generalized/unspecified anxiety.
doctor.question: Do you feel these worries are mainly a reaction to your retirement and handing off the practice?

patient.answer:
Not mainly, no. I mean, they’re certainly part of it, and I don’t want to minimize that. Retirement and handing off the practice are big changes, and they’ve given my mind plenty of material to work with.

But the worrying doesn’t feel confined to that. It spreads. I’ll start with whether my old patients are being cared for properly, then whether the handoff was financially sound, whether I missed some detail I should have caught, and then before I know it I’m thinking about what I’ll be once I’m fully retired—whether I’ll become useless, basically.

And even to me, it feels out of proportion. That’s the uncomfortable part. I can see that some concern is reasonable, but the way my mind keeps circling around it again and again feels like more than just a normal reaction to retirement.
